scenario: WIBTA for going on a trip my wife can no longer go on because of her DUI? | Last year, my wife and I made plans to spend a week in Montreal with another couple we're close friends with. None of us had been to Canada before, and we thought it would be fun if we all went together. We requested time off work, bought flights, made hotel reservations, etc. The trip is scheduled for March. Here's the problem: a month we made all these arrangements, my wife was arrested for drunk driving, and she pleaded guilty to the charge this week. My understanding is that she can no longer enter Canada with a DUI on her record. But I still want to go on the trip, which I paid a lot of money for, and I told our friends I still plan on accompanying them. My wife and I got into a huge fight over it, and she accused me of being selfish and unsupportive for wanting to go without her. I don't think that's fair. I've supported her throughout the entire court process, which has been incredibly stressful and expensive, and I've been looking forward to this trip for a long time. WIBTA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out what to do in this situation. My wife and I planned a trip to Montreal with some close friends, and we've been looking forward to it for a long time. We even went through all the hassle of requesting time off work, booking flights, and making hotel reservations. It's scheduled for March, which is just a few months away. But then, a month after we made all these arrangements, my wife got arrested for drunk driving. She pleaded guilty to the charge this week. From what I understand, having a DUI on her record means she can't enter Canada anymore. That's a big problem because we were supposed to go together. Now, I'm in a tough spot. I still want to go on the trip. I've already spent a lot of money on it, and I told our friends that I'm still planning to go with them. But my wife is really upset about this. We had a huge fight, and she accused me of being selfish and unsupportive for wanting to go without her. I don't think that's fair. I've been supporting her through the entire court process, which has been incredibly stressful and expensive. Plus, I've been looking forward to this trip for a long time. I'm wondering if I'm being selfish by wanting to go on the trip, or if it's reasonable to still want to go. I mean, I've already invested a lot of time and money into this trip, and it's something I've been excited about. But at the same time, my wife is going through a tough time, and she feels like I'm not supporting her by wanting to go without her. I guess I need to think about what's more important here: my desire to go on the trip, or my wife's feelings and the stress she's going through because of the DUI. Is it worth risking our relationship over this trip? Or should I prioritize her feelings and maybe find another way to make this work? Maybe I should talk to her again and try to understand her perspective better. She feels unsupported, and I don't want her to feel that way. But I also don't want to lose the opportunity to go on this trip, especially since we've been planning it for so long. I wonder if there's a middle ground here. Maybe we can find a way for me to go on the trip without her, but still show her that I'm supportive and that our relationship is more important than the trip. Or maybe we can reschedule the trip for a later date when she can join me. I also need to consider the financial aspect. I've already spent a lot of money on this trip, and if I cancel, I might lose some of that money. But if I go without her, I might save some of it, but I also risk damaging our relationship. It's a tough decision. I want to do what's best for both of us, but I'm not sure what that is. I need to weigh the importance of the trip against the importance of our relationship and her feelings. Maybe talking to a counselor or a trusted friend could help me see things more clearly. In the end, I think the most important thing is to communicate openly with my wife and try to find a solution that works for both of us. Whether that means rescheduling the trip, finding another way to support her while I go, or even canceling the trip altogether, I need to make sure that our relationship comes out stronger on the other side.
